I'm not sure what 'greatest' means, but I can share something I learned late in life, something that is much more useful than it probably seems at first.

You've probably heard the saying that events do not cause feelings, our interpretations of events cause feelings. This means that there is a separation - a thin sliver a daylight - between our inner state and the outer world. That separation is everything.

The usual way of describing this is to talk about the Stoic-inspired idea of how events need not disturb you, leaving you free to develop virtue despite them. That's not bad, but that's just scratching the surface.

Consider the following example: you are on vacation, you catch a rare virus, and your health declines terribly. You eventually cannot work, you can't drive, you can barely leave the house. Your days are reduced to puttering around, being a burden, being trapped and bored, with little hope for recovery. This is pretty bad, bad enough that you might consider cutting it short.

Now consider another example - you get hit by a bus, left in a coma, expected to die or be a vegetable forever. Against all odds, you wake up. Everyone is surprised and pleased to see that your brain and your personality are remarkably intact, no impairment at all. You further defy the odds and regain some use of your hands, and then enough use of your body to sit and feed yourself. A miracle. You work hard and get even better, able to walk short distances unaided, able to wash and dress yourself, able to use a computer. That's as far as you'll likely get but it feels like a gift from heaven.

The situations are identical, in the end. What differs is the narratives we tell ourselves, the arcs of the story, the categorizations we use to understand it. One is a story of hopeless decline, the other a story of miraculous rebirth. The first is full of loss and the second is full of gratitude for every little thing.

The facts that lead to the outcome are different, of course, but the stories we tell ourselves are are all bullshit. They are an imagination imposed over these facts. Life is not a story, it is just a sequence of events, and that's an entirely different thing.

You wake in the morning, and you have what you have, and you do what you think best with it. That's it. That's every day of your life, and that's been every day of your life, and you can make it a heaven or a hell as you please.

This insight goes very deep and it rewards the attention you give to it.

I'm not sure if it's particularly "great", but it's my favorite and very subtle:

wu wei - action through inaction

Taoism talks about the natural path (lol) things want to take. Water flows downhill. Dogs chase cats. Haters gonna hate. The goal of wu wei is accomplishing something with the least amount of struggling. You do this by going with the flow as much as you can to achieve your goals. If you want to go downsteam, just get a raft and float your way down. You won't even have to paddle, just lay back.

I apply this to a lot of things in my life. It saves a lot of little frustrations every day, which is why I think it's so good.

  • This ladder is resting up against a wall, but what it really wants is to be on the ground, flat. Why not just put it down to begin with? Now the wind won't knock it over and hit you later.

  • That "ding, ding, ding" noise your car makes when you left the lights on while leaving is very ingrained in us to get an "I forgot something" response - use that when designing ATM and debit card software to indicate the customer forgot their card - it'll work better than a buzz or beep noise.

  • You have a fast food place. Most other places ask "For here or to go?" as the last question before telling you the total. If your computer system requires you to ask that as the first question, you'll throw off your customers by going against their expectations. It'd be easier to change your computer system than the expectations of all your customers.

Find what is going to happen by default, find what you want to happen, then figure out how to make the two match with the least amount of fighting. Changing your goal state is one option, too.
